notes.meaning: The Israelites traveled forward and set up camp in the plains of Moab across the Jordan River from Jericho. They were now reaching the end of their forty years of wandering in the wilderness. This camp served as their staging ground before crossing the river into the Promised Land.

King Balak of Moab watched everything Israel had done to the Amorite nations. He knew the Amorite kings had been strong fighters, so their defeat proved that Israel was a powerful force. Balak realized his own army could never beat them in ordinary combat.

The Moabite people were gripped by extreme fear because the Israelites were so numerous. Their dread went so deep it made them sick with panic. In reality, God had already commanded Israel not to harm Moab, so their terror grew out of not knowing God's word.

Moab warned the leaders of Midian that this vast crowd would consume everything around them, like a hungry ox stripping grass from a field. Even though Moab and Midian had their own differences, fear led them to form a sudden partnership against Israel. They were terrified of losing all their land and supplies.

Balak sent messengers roughly four hundred miles to the Euphrates River to hire Balaam, a famous foreign seer. The king sent word that an enormous nation had come out of Egypt and covered the land right on his border. Balak hoped Balaam's spiritual reputation could rescue Moab.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: An ancient plaster wall inscription discovered at Deir Alla in Jordan mentions Balaam son of Beor as a famous seer who received divine visions by night.

notes.meaning: Balak urged Balaam to come quickly and place a curse on Israel so Moab could defeat them and drive them out. Ancient rulers often hired diviners to cast spells on enemy armies before going to battle. Balak firmly believed that whoever Balaam blessed was blessed and whoever he cursed was cursed.

The leaders of Moab and Midian set out carrying fees to pay for Balaam's divination. In the ancient world, diviners expected payment for their rituals and predictions. Bringing these fees showed that Balak treated spiritual power like a service he could purchase.

Balaam told the messengers to stay overnight while he waited to hear what the Lord would say. He recognized the name of Israel's God, who often spoke through night visions or dreams. Instead of immediately rejecting a bribe to harm God's people, Balaam opened the door to temptation.

God came to Balaam that night and asked who the men staying with him were. The Lord did not ask out of ignorance, because He knows all things. The question was meant to awaken Balaam's conscience and make him face his own dishonest motives.

Balaam answered God by reporting that King Balak of Moab had sent him a message by these visitors. Balaam knew he could hide nothing from the Lord, so he gave the king's name and royal position plainly.

Balaam repeated Balak's words about the huge crowd from Egypt that covered the ground. He explained that Balak wanted him to curse them so Moab could fight them and drive them away. Balaam gave a direct report of the request, even while keeping his own greedy desires quiet.

God gave Balaam an absolute command not to go with the messengers or curse Israel. The Lord declared that Israel was already blessed, meaning His favor could not be undone by any spell. God was protecting His covenant people from the harmful schemes of their enemies.

The next morning Balaam told the princes to return home because the Lord refused to let him go. He obeyed the order on the surface, but he never told them that God had called Israel blessed. By leaving that part out, he made it sound like he personally wanted to go if God would only let him.

The princes returned to Balak and reported only that Balaam refused to come with them. They left out any mention of the Lord's strict command. This short report led Balak to believe Balaam was merely bargaining for a higher price.

Balak sent a second group of messengers that was larger and held higher royal honor than the first. He assumed Balaam felt insulted by lower-ranking officers and wanted more flattering attention. Balak believed increased social pressure would change the seer's mind.
The high officials arrived and begged Balaam in Balak's name not to let anything keep him from coming. Balak was asking Balaam to ignore every obstacle, including the command of God Himself.

Balak promised to reward Balaam with great honor and riches and give him whatever he asked if he would just curse Israel. The king laid a massive trap for Balaam's pride and greed. When an initial temptation is not firmly rejected, it often comes back with even stronger offers.

Balaam declared that even a house filled with silver and gold could not make him disobey the Lord's word. His words sounded noble and devout, and he even spoke of the Lord as his God. Beneath this righteous speech, however, his heart still craved the wealth Balak offered.

Balaam told the nobles to spend the night so he could ask the Lord what else He might say. Since God had already given an unmistakable refusal, asking again was disrespectful and foolish. Balaam was secretly hoping God would change His mind so he could earn the promised fortune.

God came to Balaam that night and told him he could go with the men, but insisted he must only speak what God commanded. God did not change His mind or approve of Balaam's greed; He simply allowed Balaam to follow his own stubborn desires as a form of judgment. God planned to take this journey and turn it into a public blessing for Israel.
